title: Start with the simplest thing that works; add agentic complexity only when it demonstrably helps
statement: Reach for the simplest design first (a single call, a fixed workflow) and add autonomous-agent complexity only when a simpler solution demonstrably falls short, because agency trades latency and cost for flexibility you may not need.
rationale: Autonomous loops add latency, token cost, and compounding-error risk. If a task decomposes into fixed steps, a workflow is more predictable and cheaper; agency only pays off when the path cannot be predicted in advance.
applies_when: Designing any new LLM feature or loop
The task's steps are largely predictable
not_when: The number and nature of steps genuinely cannot be predicted (then an agent is warranted)
how: State the task as a fixed workflow first and see if it suffices
Introduce dynamic tool-use/looping only against a measured shortfall of the workflow
Keep the agent-computer interface small and well-documented if you do go agentic
check: Can you point to a measured failure of a simpler workflow that justifies the current agentic complexity? If not, it is unjustified.
failure_if_absent: Teams build multi-step autonomous systems where a single optimized call would have been cheaper, faster, and easier to debug.

evidence.title: Anthropic - Building Effective Agents
evidence.quote: we recommend finding the simplest solution possible, and only increasing complexity when needed
evidence.note: Anthropic's summarized first principle: build the right system, not the most sophisticated one.
